the fate and transport of radionuclides in the vadose zone of the Hanford site, which is contaminated by high-level nuclear waste.
the geochemical fate of contaminants in sediments weathered by hyperalkalinity.

the sorption of Sr and Cs to the neo-formed aluminates, feldspathoids, and aluminosilicate minerals is the dominant mechanism of sequestration of these radionuclides at the Hanford Site.

the sorption of Sr and Cs to neo-formed aluminates and aluminosilicate minerals is a long-term sequestration mechanism, but that dissolution of these phases can also be a source for contaminant release.

the formation of neo-formed minerals in the presence of HLRW is an effective mechanism for sequestering (137)Cs, (90)Sr, and (129)I, but that the dissolution of these minerals may result in a long-term supply of these contaminants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the long-term fate of Sr and Cs is controlled by the formation of neo-formed minerals during hyperalkaline weathering and that the long-term persistence and mobility of these contaminants is controlled by the mineralogic composition of the weathering products.

The main takeaway from our work is that
mineral sorption/coprecpitation is not a permanent sink for contaminants.
the long-term fate of radionuclides in hyperalkaline environments depends not only on the initial geochemical environment but also on the subsequent geochemical evolution of the system.
